analysis.one_liner: Waives federal royalties on deep-water oil and gas drilled in the Gulf of Mexico.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it drew one hearing in March 1995 and never came to a Senate vote, with a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Oil and gas beneath the Gulf of Mexico belongs to the federal government, and companies leasing it pay a royalty — a share of the value of what they pump — to the Treasury. This bill would let those companies skip that royalty on deep-water production: existing leases could have royalties reduced or eliminated, and new deep-water leases would pay no royalty until the company had pumped a minimum volume of oil — at least 17.5 million barrels of oil equivalent in 200-400 meters of water, and 87.5 million barrels in water deeper than 800 meters. Relief would stop, in most cases, only if oil averaged above $28 a barrel or gas above $3.50 per million BTU.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that lease deep-water Gulf tracts and drill there. They would pump the first tens of millions of barrels from a lease without paying the government its share, converting public-resource revenue into company profit. Bill text and the CRS summary also allow royalty terms on existing leases to be reduced or eliminated before production starts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Deep-water Gulf oil and gas producers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would suspend royalties on new deep-water Gulf leases until specified volumes are produced — at least 17.5 million barrels of oil equivalent in 200-400 meters of water, 52.5 million in 400-800 meters, and 87.5 million in water deeper than 800 meters.
It would also let the Interior Secretary reduce or eliminate royalties on existing deep-water leases before production begins, where deep-water development is judged uneconomic without relief.

Supporters framed this as encouraging domestic oil and gas production in deep water to strengthen national energy security, on the theory that lower upfront costs make risky, expensive deep-water projects viable.
The relief includes price triggers: royalties would apply in any year oil averaged above $28 a barrel or natural gas above $3.50 per million BTU, limiting the giveaway when prices are high.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. Royalties on offshore oil and gas are Treasury revenue from resources the public owns, so every royalty-free barrel is revenue the government never collects — money that would otherwise help fund the government generally and, historically, programs like land and water conservation.

drawbacks.text: The bill forgives revenue from publicly owned oil and gas. Deep-water fields are large, so the royalty-free volumes specified in the bill — up to 87.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per lease — represent substantial forgone Treasury income.
The price triggers are set high: relief continues until oil averages over $28 a barrel or gas over $3.50 per million BTU, so companies keep the royalty break in ordinary price conditions.

The Treasury still receives a minimum 12.5% royalty on new leases once relief volumes are exhausted, and an economic test can deny relief to production that would be profitable anyway — but the Secretary's determination is final agency action with only a 30-day window for court challenges, limiting oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case is that deep-water drilling was genuinely expensive and risky in 1995, and a royalty holiday can tip marginal projects into production — with the price triggers and minimum 12.5% royalty as real limits. But the design hands out blanket, volume-based relief to all qualifying deep-water production, not just projects that need it, and the cost is paid not by an industry but by the public in forgone revenue from its own oil and gas. The public gets domestic production in exchange for giving away part of the value of a resource it owns.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got one hearing in March 1995, and never came back out for a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. J. Bennett Johnston of Louisiana introduced the bill on January 5, 1995, with introductory remarks, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The committee held hearings on March 23, 1995 — the last action the bill ever received.
The bill died with a single cosponsor and no roll-call vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Short-term, the Treasury and taxpayers, who kept collecting royalties under existing rules because this bill died. But the broader story is more mixed: substantially similar deep-water royalty relief was enacted later in 1995 through separate legislation signed by President Clinton (widely reported; not in the provided sources), so the industry largely got the policy anyway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers kept royalties; industry won elsewhere

for.name: Sen. J. Bennett Johnston
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill, held a single hearing on March 23, 1995, and never reported it to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, so no partisan pattern shows up in the record.

industries.industry: Deep-water Gulf of Mexico oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill would let producers pump tens of millions of barrels of publicly owned oil and gas without paying royalties, converting Treasury revenue into company margin. The public's cost is the government's forgone share of its own resource.

industries.industry: Oil-field services and offshore drilling contractors
industries.note: Relief is intended to spur expensive deep-water development projects, which would mean more offshore drilling and construction work. The benefit to these industries comes from activity paid for by forgone public revenue.
